episode_thesis: Alan Dunn argues that markets face a collision of two unprecedented shocks, an AI positive supply shock that also brings an inflationary capex demand impulse and an Iran-war energy supply shock, which leaves central banks in a dilemma, pushes governments toward fiscal dominance, and can hit stocks and bonds together; that the answer is a portfolio pairing strategic beta with a large trend sleeve that works as transparent tactical asset allocation. Niels adds that trend and macro opportunity may depend on inflation instability rather than rate activity, that markets are increasingly flow- and positioning-driven, and that unconstrained trend including equities suits that world. Dunn announces the Regime Adaptive Fund built on this logic.

worldview_premises.premise: AI capex distorts US growth and earnings data: growth and index earnings are concentrated (Mag 7), labor share is at a record low, and much capex leaks abroad as imports, so headline figures overstate breadth.
worldview_premises.support: Greg Ip (WSJ) calculations: AI economy up 31% in Q1 vs non-AI flat; Q1 earnings up 27% with Mag 7 up 61% and the rest 16%; labor share 54%, lowest since 1947; 33 counties hold 72% of data centers.

worldview_premises.premise: An AI bust would not be benign because falling equity prices would hit consumption through the wealth effect.
worldview_premises.support: Criticism of the Ip article's 'little impact' conclusion.

worldview_premises.premise: An oil-price spike from Middle East conflict is an adverse supply shock (stagflationary) that hurts both bonds and equities; the 1970s had negative real returns in both, so stagflation breaks 60/40 diversification.
worldview_premises.support: Standard aggregate supply framework; 1970s history.

worldview_premises.premise: Central banks normally look through energy shocks unless second-round effects emerge, but after COVID inflation households are more price-sensitive so expectations may de-anchor; 2008 showed they can mis-respond.
worldview_premises.support: 2008 ECB hike in May then cuts by October; COVID experience.

worldview_premises.premise: Energy shocks have uneven effects: the US is probably more insulated than Europe or Asia, and lower-income households are hit hardest, creating pressure for subsidies.
worldview_premises.support: Fuel's larger budget share for low-income households.

worldview_premises.premise: AI is a positive supply shock (disinflationary in theory) but also an inflationary demand impulse via capex (hyperscaler spending near USD 1 trillion a year), as in the 1990s when Greenspan eventually hiked; both AI and energy shocks occurring together has no precedent.
worldview_premises.support: 1990s analogy; hyperscaler earnings guidance.

worldview_premises.premise: Shocks and high debt bias governments toward more spending (subsidies, defence, AI-displacement support), pushing economies toward fiscal dominance, and rising yields can start a vicious cycle on debt service.
worldview_premises.support: UK gilt yields above 5% before falling after local elections; US troop withdrawal from Germany raising European defence spending.

worldview_premises.premise: Macro alpha is higher when central banks are more active and policy cycles diverge; macro beats 60/40 before hikes and does better after cuts and in easing cycles (which are typically recessions).
worldview_premises.support: Graham Capital 'macro across monetary regimes' paper.

worldview_premises.premise: The size and volatility of interest-rate moves is the main driver of trend and macro opportunity; high rates that start to fall give strong fixed-income trends and a steep curve gives carry; surprise inflation may matter more than the level.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning about the 1980s-90s fixed-income trend; he doubts that inflation and rates can be separated empirically.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend is a simple, transparent, systematic form of tactical asset allocation, insurance-like in bear markets yet with a positive long-term return; conventional TAA tilts (60 to 57) are marginal.
worldview_premises.support: AQR's Jordan Brooks interview in the Journal of Finance.

worldview_premises.premise: Bonds fall with core and food-and-energy inflation; equities tolerate food-and-energy inflation but struggle with core inflation (2022); commodities gain from food and energy; a stock-bond portfolio is short inflation risk so needs trend and commodities.
worldview_premises.support: Brooks's research.

worldview_premises.premise: Portfolio construction is optimisation of objectives under constraints; a broader universe, long-short and leverage (return stacking) raise the opportunity set.
worldview_premises.support: Jordan Brooks interview.

worldview_premises.premise: Even well-diversified portfolios occasionally lose in all components by chance (March 2026, 'death by a thousand cuts'); whether trend and macro profit from a rate shock depends on initial positioning; this is the price of avoiding a large equity bear market.
worldview_premises.support: March 2026 rate shock vs 2022 comparison.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend in an asset class is a different premium from the asset's own beta, stems from behavioural biases and works better across many markets, so trend should trade equities even when stacked on equity beta.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning; trend modulates equity exposure while diversifying.

worldview_premises.premise: Narratives explaining trend performance are post hoc; strong runs cannot be anticipated but recur, so do not time trend allocations on stories.
worldview_premises.support: A conference where the same speakers explained poor trend performance 12 months earlier.

worldview_premises.premise: 'Stay invested' is a weak message because the real risk is a 50% equity drawdown or lost decade; trend embeds a systematic response, and investors struggle to hold trend because returns come in lumps.
worldview_premises.support: Investor conversations; 2008 and 1970s examples.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Ledger fixes applied: the 'equities since 2009' point belongs to Niels, and the Alan statement on oil shocks said only that the US is probably more insulated than Europe or Asia.
Alan's critique of the Ip article assumes a wealth-effect channel but gives no magnitude; the AI-bust argument is qualitative.
The macro-alpha findings come from Graham Capital papers relayed second-hand; effect sizes (e.g. macro better 'in the double digits' of hikes and cuts) are not stated.
Alan says macro outperforms before hikes but also notes easing cycles are the strongest regime; which regime dominates today (hike risk vs recession) is not resolved.
Trend premium is said to stem from behavioural biases, but no evidence is offered; the Regime Adaptive Fund's historical benefits are described without numbers.
Niels says trend made little money in the 2009 equity bull market and also wants equities in the program; Alan says trend probably made money; neither provides data.
The statement that trend and macro lost in March 2026 and gained in 2022 'just by virtue of initial positioning' is not tested; Niels also reports a quick April recovery to new highs.
The 'impact on construction employment' claim and 'imports to Korea' leakage derive from one journalist's calculations and are not verified.
Niels admits his flows-versus-macro view and optimism about trend are biased.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs the speakers say lead prices: energy prices and the market's willingness to keep looking through the Middle East shock; central bank reaction to energy-driven inflation (look through vs de-anchoring expectations); AI capex (hyperscaler guidance) as a demand impulse and its financing or unwind; fiscal pressure and government yields (UK gilts above 5%); dispersion of policy cycles (Fed, ECB, BOJ, UK) for macro opportunity; inflation instability and long-end yields; positioning and flows (steepener crowding, cocoa short covering). Horizons range from weeks (positioning) to years (fiscal dominance, regime change).
reader_inferences: (reader) Dunn's thesis chains three shocks (energy, AI capex, fiscal response) to one portfolio conclusion: since forecasting which regime wins is impossible, hold beta and a trend sleeve that reprices when the regime shows itself, which is also why he stresses that narratives about trend are post hoc.

(reader) The disagreement on inflation stability versus rate volatility is partly semantic: both say opportunity needs large, uncertain moves in rates or inflation; the 2010s are the shared counterexample.

(reader) The announcement of the Regime Adaptive Fund colours Dunn's choice of evidence: the Brooks interview, Graham paper and diversification-discomfort framing all support a trend-plus-beta wrapper for wealth investors; the speakers say this is their stated philosophy.
(reader) Niels's flows-and-positioning view and Dunn's crowded-steepener explanation of the March rate shock agree on mechanism: positioning, not news, amplified the move.
